notes: Catholic women's liberal-arts college in New Orleans, Louisiana, chartered 1910 by the Dominican Sisters; disbanded in 1984, its grounds sold to Loyola University New Orleans (now Loyola's Broadway campus). Source states no cause.

name: Southern Bible College
notes: Pentecostal Bible college in Houston, Texas, founded 1958 under the East Texas District of the Pentecostal Church of God; closed May 1984 for financial reasons.

name: University of South Dakota-Springfield
notes: Public college in Springfield, South Dakota, founded 1881 as Southern State Normal School; though financially viable, the state closed it in July 1984 and converted the campus to the Mike Durfee State Prison amid a prison-space shortage.

name: Whitworth Female College
notes: Methodist women's college in Brookhaven, Mississippi, founded 1858 (two-year from 1928); in 1938, facing financial difficulty, its trustees voted to cease operations and merge into the still-operating Millsaps College. It appears in Wikipedia's 1984 disestablished category, but 1984 marks only the end of later unrelated tenancies on the campus.

name: Nasson College
notes: Liberal-arts college in Springvale (Sanford), Maine, founded 1912 (four-year from 1935); enrollment collapsed after the Vietnam War and it ran out of funds, closing 1983. A brief mid-1980s revival failed and was not a successor.

name: Northwood University-West Baden
notes: Satellite business-management campus of the still-operating Northwood University, opened 1966 under the dome of the former West Baden Springs Hotel in West Baden Springs, Indiana; closed 1983. Source states no cause.

name: Soule Business College
notes: Proprietary business college in New Orleans, Louisiana, founded 1856; it continued after its founder's death until finally closing in 1983 (it enrolled upwards of 40,000 students by 1922). Source states no cause.

name: Vesper George School of Art
notes: Art school in Boston, Massachusetts, founded 1924; closed 1983. Source states neither control nor cause.

name: Colegio Cesar Chavez
notes: The first accredited, independent four-year Chicano/Latino college in the United States, in Mount Angel, Oregon, founded 1973 out of the earlier Mt. Angel College; closed 1983 amid financial and administrative problems and reduced federal support.

name: Clarksville School of Theology
notes: Theological seminary in Clarksville, Tennessee (later Clayton, North Carolina); shut down by an August 2, 1982 court decision after its curriculum was found not to meet state standards for granting a degree. Source states no founding year.

name: La Salle Extension University
notes: For-profit correspondence university in Chicago, Illinois, founded 1908 (owned by Crowell-Collier from 1961); it enrolled more than 100,000 students in 1969, lost its law-school program to FTC action in 1980, and closed in 1982. Source states no single cause.

name: Cooper School of Art
notes: For-profit commercial-art school in Cleveland, Ohio, founded 1924; closed 1981 in a financial and administrative crisis (unpaid wages, lawsuits, code violations).

name: Immaculate Heart College
notes: Catholic college in Los Angeles, California, founded 1905 by the Sisters of the Immaculate Heart of Mary; closed 1981 amid financial difficulties.

name: Durham College (North Carolina)
notes: Junior college in Durham, North Carolina, founded 1946; its accreditation was revoked in August 1979 and it closed in October 1980. Wikipedia does not specify nonprofit vs for-profit control.

name: Edgecliff College
notes: Catholic women's liberal-arts college in Cincinnati, Ohio, founded 1935; after financial struggles it merged July 1, 1980 into the still-operating Xavier University (final class 1984).

name: Saint Gregory Seminary
notes: Roman Catholic minor seminary (high-school and college seminary) in the Mount Washington district of Cincinnati, Ohio, founded 1890 under the Archdiocese of Cincinnati; closed 1980 over declining enrollment, remaining students transferring to the Pontifical College Josephinum.

name: Detroit College of Business
notes: Business college in Dearborn, Michigan, founded 1962; merged in 2000 with Davenport College and Great Lakes College to form the still-operating Davenport University, retiring the name. Wikipedia does not state nonprofit vs for-profit control.

name: George Williams College (Chicago)
notes: YMCA-rooted college founded 1890 in Chicago, Illinois (later at Williams Bay, Wisconsin); affiliated with Aurora University in 1992 and formally merged into the still-operating Aurora University in 2000.

name: United States International University
notes: Private university in San Diego, California, founded 1924; financial strain from international expansion and lost enrollment after September 11 led to a 2001 merger with the California School of Professional Psychology to form the still-operating Alliant International University.

name: Allegheny University of the Health Sciences
notes: Philadelphia health-sciences university (the renamed MCP/Hahnemann), the first US medical school to declare bankruptcy (July 21, 1998) amid the collapse of its parent AHERF; its medical school passed to the still-operating Drexel University around 2002.

name: Notre Dame College (New Hampshire)
notes: Catholic college in Manchester, New Hampshire, founded 1950 by the Sisters of Holy Cross; closed May 2002 amid enrollment and financial difficulty, its programs transferring to Southern New Hampshire University. Distinct from the Ohio Notre Dame College.

name: Trinity College of Vermont
notes: Catholic college in Burlington, Vermont, founded 1925 by the Sisters of Mercy; closed in 2000 under financial constraints, the University of Vermont buying its campus.

name: Decker College
notes: For-profit career college in Louisville, Kentucky (5,700 students); closed September 2005 and filed bankruptcy after the U.S. Department of Education terminated its accreditation and aid over its construction and online courses (a 2016 federal court later found the termination rested on false allegations).

name: D-Q University
notes: Independent tribal two-year college near Davis, California, founded 1971; ended full-time classes in 2005 after losing accreditation amid enrollment decline and loss of BIA and federal funding.

name: Henry Cogswell College
notes: Private college in Everett, Washington, founded 1979 (initially tied to Cogswell College of Sunnyvale, California); closed September 1, 2006 amid enrollment decline and a substantial deficit. Wikipedia says only 'private' as to control.

name: H. Sophie Newcomb Memorial College
notes: Women's coordinate college of the still-operating Tulane University in New Orleans, founded 1886 (the first degree-granting coordinate college for women in the US); dissolved into the co-educational Newcomb-Tulane College on July 1, 2006 in a reorganization forced by Hurricane Katrina losses.

name: Pacific Western University (Hawaii)
notes: Unaccredited distance university in Hawaii, founded 1988; the State of Hawaii sued it and a court ordered it to cease operations in May 2006 with a $500,000 penalty. Recorded as a closure with a diploma-mill caveat.

name: Crown College (Tacoma)
notes: For-profit college in Tacoma, Washington, founded 1990; lost accreditation July 31, 2007 for failing graduate-placement standards and suspended operations August 10, 2007 (former officers were later indicted for aid fraud). Distinct from the operating Crown College in Minnesota.

name: New College of California
notes: Progressive private college in San Francisco, California, founded 1971 (with a law school); WASC revoked its accreditation in February 2008 over governance, records, and oversight failures and it closed, individual programs dispersing to other schools.

name: TransPacific Hawaii College
notes: Two-year college in Honolulu, Hawaii, founded 1977 (250 students); closed December 31, 2008 after its accreditor faulted a financial structure that depended on tuition income (records held by Kansai Gaidai University). Wikipedia does not state nonprofit vs for-profit control.

name: Woodbury College
notes: College in Montpelier, Vermont, founded 1975 (associate degrees from 1993, bachelor's from 2000); merged in August 2008 into the still-operating Champlain College, its 125 students transferring. Source states no cause or nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: Katharine Gibbs School - Melville
notes: Long Island campus (Melville, New York) of the for-profit Katharine Gibbs School / Gibbs College chain; closed December 8, 2008, the site becoming a Sanford-Brown Institute. Source states no cause or campus-opening year.

name: Biscayne Southern College
notes: Private college in Concord, North Carolina (branches in Charlotte and Gastonia), operating 1948-2004 (526 students in 1983). Source states no cause or nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: National Radio Institute
notes: For-profit home-study electronics school in Washington, D.C., founded 1914 (accredited by the National Home Study Council, ~60,000 students in the mid-1980s, owned by McGraw-Hill from 1968); it stopped enrollments in 1999 and discontinued operations March 31, 2002 as electronics became disposable.

name: Southeastern Institute of Technology
notes: Private nonprofit graduate professional school in Huntsville, Alabama, founded 1976; its board placed it in inactive status in 2004 after finding its original purpose duplicated by other schools.

name: Arizona International College
notes: Public liberal-arts college in Tucson, Arizona, founded 1996; it became a college within the still-operating University of Arizona in 1998 and was disestablished in November 2001 amid post-9/11 budget cuts, its students absorbed into other UofA faculties.

name: Huron University
notes: Private university in Huron, South Dakota, founded 1883; its Huron campus closed April 1, 2005 amid financial mismanagement and foreclosure (its separate London campus continued independently). Records held by Northern State University.

name: Sacred Heart College (North Carolina)
notes: Catholic women's college in Belmont, North Carolina, run by the Sisters of Mercy, founded 1892; closed in 1987 after years of declining enrollment, its facilities passing to Belmont Abbey College. Distinct from same-named colleges elsewhere.

name: University of Albuquerque
notes: Catholic university in Albuquerque, New Mexico, founded 1920 (3,200 students in 1972); closed at the end of the 1986 spring semester amid mounting debt and new two-year-degree competition, records going to the University of New Mexico.

name: Antioch School of Law
parent_name: District of Columbia School of Law
notes: Public-interest law school in Washington, D.C., founded 1972 under Antioch University; after its parent could no longer sustain it, it was reconstituted in 1986 as the public District of Columbia School of Law (now the UDC David A. Clarke School of Law).

name: O. W. Coburn School of Law
notes: Law school of the still-operating Oral Roberts University in Tulsa, Oklahoma, founded 1979; closed in 1986, its law library, five professors, and 23 students moving to CBN University (renamed Regent University in 1990). Source states no cause.

name: Tift College
notes: Georgia Baptist women's college in Forsyth, Georgia, tracing to 1849 (Forsyth Female Collegiate Institute, later Bessie Tift College); merged into the still-operating Mercer University in 1986, ceasing operations in 1987. Source states no cause.

name: Nathaniel Hawthorne College
notes: Private college in Antrim, New Hampshire, founded 1962 (peak enrollment 800 in 1971); despite a 1982 tie to the Florida Institute of Technology it carried over $4 million in debt and declared bankruptcy, closing in 1988.

name: Swain School of Design
notes: Art and design school in New Bedford, Massachusetts, founded 1881 (the 12th-oldest US art school); low enrollment led to a 1988 merger into Southeastern Massachusetts University, now the still-operating University of Massachusetts Dartmouth.

name: Wang Institute of Graduate Studies
notes: Graduate software-engineering institute in Tyngsborough, Massachusetts, founded 1979 by An Wang of Wang Laboratories; closed August 27, 1988 when its benefactor's declining business fortunes ended the funding (campus went to Boston University).

name: Benjamin Franklin University
notes: Accountancy college in Washington, D.C., founded 1925 (successor to Pace's DC campus); merged into the still-operating George Washington University in August 1987 after a DC accountancy board imposed liberal-arts and faculty requirements it could not afford.

name: Seminex
parent_name: Lutheran School of Theology at Chicago
notes: Lutheran seminary in St. Louis, Missouri ('Concordia Seminary in Exile'), formed 1974 in a Missouri Synod doctrinal walkout; its last St. Louis class graduated 1983 and it formally dissolved into the Lutheran School of Theology at Chicago in 1987 (faculty also to Wartburg and Pacific Lutheran seminaries).

name: Windham College
notes: Private liberal-arts college in Putney, Vermont, founded 1951 (peak enrollment 935); post-Vietnam enrollment fell to 254 and it closed in 1978, its campus later becoming Landmark College.

name: Concordia Senior College
notes: Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod upper-division college in Fort Wayne, Indiana, founded 1957; in 1977 the LCMS transferred its function to other Concordia system colleges and the campus became home to Concordia Theological Seminary.

name: St. Charles College (Maryland)
notes: Sulpician minor seminary (a college-level junior college) in Catonsville, Maryland (originally Ellicott City), founded 1830; its junior college merged into St. Mary's Seminary and University in 1969 and the Catonsville site closed in 1977 (it appears in Wikipedia's 1977 category on the site-closure date).

name: Washington Technical Institute
parent_name: University of the District of Columbia
notes: Public technical institute in Washington, D.C.; merged August 1, 1977 with Federal City College and DC Teachers College to form the still-operating University of the District of Columbia. Source states no founding year.

name: Southeastern Christian College
notes: Churches of Christ junior college in Winchester, Kentucky, founded 1949 (incorporated 1950); closed in 1979 for lack of funds, its campus becoming a county park.

name: Southern Benedictine College
notes: Catholic Benedictine college at St. Bernard, Cullman, Alabama, founded 1893 as St. Bernard College (a four-year college after 1955; renamed Southern Benedictine after a 1976 merger with Cullman College); closed May 13, 1979. Source states no cause.

name: St. Anthony College (Hudson, New Hampshire)
notes: Capuchin Franciscan bachelor's-degree seminary college in Hudson, New Hampshire, founded circa 1954; closed 1979. Stub source states no cause.

name: Dakota Business College
notes: Family-owned proprietary business college in Fargo, North Dakota, founded 1890 by F. Leland Watkins and still Watkins-owned when it closed in 1978. Source states no cause.

name: Franconia College
notes: Experimental liberal-arts college in Franconia, New Hampshire, founded 1963 (four-year from 1965, peak enrollment 400 in 1972); after years of declining enrollment it went bankrupt and closed January 23, 1978.

name: Ricker College
notes: Private liberal-arts college in Houlton, Maine, founded 1848 (a junior college 1934-1978, four-year thereafter); closed May 1978 amid the financial pressure on small private colleges.

name: Elkhart University
notes: Proprietary school of medical and dental laboratory technology in Elkhart, Indiana, founded 1882 (earlier Elkhart Business University / Institute of Technology); closed in 1986 after 104 years due to financial difficulties.

name: International College (Los Angeles)
notes: Non-traditional tutorial college in Los Angeles, California, founded 1970 (350 students in 1980); it had no campus and never attained accreditation, closing in 1986 with students transferring to the (also unaccredited) William Lyon University. Recorded with an unaccredited caveat.

name: Cornell School of Nursing
notes: Nursing school in New York City tracing to 1877, from 1942 the Cornell University-New York Hospital School of Nursing; the still-operating Cornell University ended the program with its last class in 1979 after a planning review found enough regional nursing programs existed.

name: Grahm Junior College
notes: Junior college in Boston, Massachusetts, founded 1951 (nonprofit from 1968; peak enrollment 1,300); filed for bankruptcy reorganization in 1977 and closed in summer 1979, its programs partly absorbed by Mount Ida College.

name: Carver Junior College (Florida)
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Cocoa, Florida, founded 1960; merged in 1963 amid low enrollment into what became Brevard Community College, now the still-operating Eastern Florida State College.

name: Seneca Junior College
notes: Baptist school for African American students in Seneca, South Carolina, founded 1899 as the Seneca Institute; it added two years of college work in 1926 to become Seneca Junior College and closed in 1939 after struggling through the Depression.

name: Barnett Hospital and Nursing School
notes: Diploma nursing school of the Black Barnett Hospital in Huntington, West Virginia, opened 1918; the nursing school closed in 1939 (the hospital continued under later ownership). Source states no cause or nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: Cotner College
notes: Disciples of Christ college at Bethany Heights (Lincoln), Nebraska, founded 1889; closed in 1933 amid Depression finances, continuing afterward only as a non-degree school of religion.

name: Lincoln and Lee University
notes: Methodist university chartered 1927 in Kansas City, Missouri; it never fully operated independently and, after the 1929 crash left its fundraising far short, merged in 1933 into the University of Kansas City (now the still-operating University of Missouri-Kansas City).

name: Spokane University
notes: Restoration Movement college in Spokane, Washington, founded 1912; Depression finances led it to merge in 1934 with Eugene Bible College to form Northwest Christian College, now the still-operating Bushnell University. Distinct from the separate Spokane College.

name: Santa Barbara School of the Arts
notes: Art college in Santa Barbara, California, founded 1920 by the painter Fernand Lungren (1857-1932); closed in 1933. Stub source states no cause.

name: Hartshorn Memorial College
notes: Baptist college for Black women in Richmond, Virginia, founded 1883 (in 1892 the first US Black women's college to confer baccalaureate degrees); merged in 1932 into the still-operating Virginia Union University.

name: Lane Seminary
notes: Presbyterian theological seminary in Walnut Hills, Cincinnati, Ohio, founded 1829 (famed for the 1834 'Lane Rebels' antislavery debates); under financial pressure it merged in 1932 into the still-operating McCormick Theological Seminary in Chicago.

name: University of Wisconsin Experimental College
notes: Experimental two-year undergraduate program (Alexander Meiklejohn's) within the still-operating University of Wisconsin-Madison, founded 1927; the regents voted to end it in 1932 amid low enrollment and Depression pressure.

name: Kentucky College for Women
notes: Women's college in Danville, Kentucky, founded 1860; a department of Centre College from 1926, it officially merged into the still-operating Centre College in 1930 as its women's division.

name: Little Rock College
notes: Roman Catholic college in Little Rock, Arkansas, founded 1908; closed in 1930, its campus later becoming the site of Catholic High School for Boys. Source states no cause.

name: Missouri Wesleyan College
notes: Methodist college in Cameron, Missouri, founded 1883 (opened as Cameron Institute); merged with the still-operating Baker University in 1926 and closed its Cameron operation in 1930. Stub source states no cause.

name: Teachers College of Indianapolis
notes: Privately funded teacher-training college in Indianapolis, Indiana, founded 1882 by Eliza A. Blaker; merged in 1930 into the still-operating Butler University as part of its school of education. Source states no cause.

name: Logan College
notes: Methodist college in Russellville, Kentucky, operating 1856-1931 (a finishing school, then a four-year college, and a junior college in its final years); a 1930 merger attempt with Kentucky Wesleyan College failed and it closed in May 1931. Source states no cause.

name: McTyeire College
notes: Methodist college in McKenzie, Tennessee, tracing to 1858 (Caledonia College, then McKenzie College, then McTyeire from 1882); closed in 1931. Stub source states no cause.

name: Episcopal Theological Seminary of the Caribbean
notes: Episcopal Church seminary in San Juan, Puerto Rico, founded 1961; closed 1976. Source states no cause.

name: Garland Junior College
notes: Women's junior college in Boston, Massachusetts, founded 1872; in March 1976 its trustees voted to transfer the college's name, facilities, and assets to the still-operating Simmons College.

name: Saint Edward Seminary
notes: Roman Catholic seminary in Kenmore, Washington, founded 1931 (a minor seminary, with a major seminary from 1935); closed in 1976 over declining enrollment, the grounds becoming Saint Edward State Park.

name: University of Plano
notes: Private liberal-arts college in Plano, Texas, founded 1964; heavily reliant on land speculation, it could not fund operations after the 1975 land boom ended and closed in 1976 (its article also gives an end date of 1977). Source does not state nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: Butte Business College
notes: Proprietary business college in Butte, Montana, founded 1890; unable to obtain loans to fund operations, it closed April 12, 1975.

name: John F. Kennedy College
notes: Private college in Wahoo, Nebraska, founded 1965 (one of six colleges built on the Parsons College model); enrollment fell after the 1973 end of the draft and, with financial trouble and fires, it closed in 1975. Source does not state nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: Lowell Technological Institute
notes: Public technical institute in Lowell, Massachusetts, founded 1895 as the Lowell Textile School; merged in 1975 with Lowell State College to form the University of Lowell, now the still-operating University of Massachusetts Lowell.

name: Mary Manse College
notes: Catholic (Ursuline) women's college in Toledo, Ohio, founded 1922 (coeducational from 1971); hit by the 1970s recession, it declared bankruptcy and closed in 1975.

name: Dominican College of Racine
notes: Catholic (Dominican) college in Racine, Wisconsin, tracing to 1864 (St. Catherine's Female Academy; a four-year college from 1946, renamed College of Racine in 1972); closed 1974. Source states no cause.

name: Episcopal Theological School
notes: Episcopal seminary in Cambridge, Massachusetts, founded 1867; merged in 1974 with the Philadelphia Divinity School to form the Episcopal Divinity School (which itself ceased granting degrees in 2017).

name: Marillac College
notes: Catholic (Daughters of Charity) women's college in the Normandy area of St. Louis, Missouri, founded 1955; closed 1974, its campus later acquired by the University of Missouri-St. Louis. Source states no cause.

name: Philadelphia Divinity School
notes: Episcopal seminary in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, founded 1857; merged in 1974 with the Episcopal Theological School to form the Episcopal Divinity School in Cambridge, Massachusetts (which itself ceased granting degrees in 2017).

name: Woodstock College
notes: Jesuit theologate in Woodstock, Maryland (later New York City), founded 1869; closed in 1974 as the order consolidated its theology schools nationally, succeeded by the Woodstock Theological Center research institute at Georgetown.

name: California Concordia College
notes: Lutheran (LCMS) junior college in Oakland, California, founded 1906 (with a high-school component); closed 1973, its records held by Concordia University Irvine. Source states no cause.

name: Dunbarton College of the Holy Cross
notes: Catholic women's college in Washington, D.C., founded 1935 by the Sisters of the Holy Cross; closed 1973, its campus bought by Howard University for its law school. Source states no cause.

name: Malcolm X Liberation University
notes: Black-nationalist college in Durham, then Greensboro, North Carolina, founded 1969; closed June 28, 1973 amid insufficient funding and internal disagreement.

name: Margaret Morrison Carnegie College
notes: Women's college of the Carnegie Institute of Technology (now the still-operating Carnegie Mellon University) in Pittsburgh, founded 1903; closed 1973 as enrollment fell, its programs absorbed into CMU's other colleges.

name: Southwood College
notes: Private college in Salemburg, North Carolina, tracing to 1874 (formed in 1965 from Edwards Military Institute and Pineland College); closed 1973. Stub source states no cause.

name: Bliss College (Maine)
notes: For-profit business and junior college in Lewiston, Maine, operating 1897-1972; closed in bankruptcy. Distinct from the separate Bliss College in Columbus, Ohio.

name: Siena College (Tennessee)
notes: Catholic (Dominican) women's college in Memphis, Tennessee, founded 1922 as St. Agnes College (the first Catholic women's college in the Memphis area); closed 1972. Source states no cause.

name: College of Artesia
notes: Private liberal-arts college in Artesia, New Mexico, founded 1966 as a Parsons College satellite; like all the 'Parsons Plan' schools it proved economically unviable and closed in 1971.

name: John J. Pershing College
notes: Private liberal-arts college in Beatrice, Nebraska, founded 1966 as a Parsons College satellite; closed in 1971 amid the 'Parsons Plan' collapse.

name: Monticello College
notes: Women's college in Godfrey, Illinois, founded 1838 (among the oldest women's colleges in America); in 1970-71 the new Lewis and Clark Community College District took over its grounds, buildings, and faculty. No standalone Wikipedia article (facts from the Lewis and Clark Community College page).

name: Mount St. Scholastica College
notes: Catholic Benedictine women's college in Atchison, Kansas, founded 1923; merged July 1, 1971 with St. Benedict's College to form the still-operating Benedictine College.

name: Pembroke College (Brown University)
notes: Women's coordinate college of the still-operating Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, founded 1891; fully merged into Brown on July 1, 1971.

name: Cape Cod Hospital School of Nursing
notes: Diploma nursing school of the still-operating Cape Cod Hospital in Hyannis, Massachusetts, running from the mid-1940s until 1971. Source (a single sentence) states no cause or founding year.

name: North Dakota State Normal and Industrial School
notes: Public normal and industrial school in Ellendale, North Dakota, founded 1899 and a branch of the University of North Dakota from 1965; a 1970 fire destroyed two main buildings and the state declined to rebuild, closing it in 1971.

name: Detroit Institute of Musical Arts
notes: Music conservatory in Detroit, Michigan, providing higher music education from 1914 to 1970; in 1970 it merged with the Detroit Music Settlement School to form the Detroit Community Music School.

name: Orlando Junior College
notes: Private junior college in Orlando, Florida, founded 1941; its viability was undercut by the 1967 founding of public Valencia College and it closed in 1970, the site becoming Lake Highland Preparatory School.

name: College of Saint Mary-of-the-Wasatch
notes: Catholic women's college in Salt Lake City, Utah, founded 1875 by the Sisters of the Holy Cross; closed 1969 (buildings demolished 1972). Source states no cause.

name: Magic Valley Christian College
notes: Churches of Christ college in Albion, Idaho, founded 1958; after the spring 1969 term it closed the Albion campus and relocated to Baker City, Oregon, as Baker College, citing the small local Churches of Christ community.

name: Diocesan Sisters College
notes: Catholic diocesan college in Bloomfield, Connecticut, founded 1949 to train nuns as teachers; closed 1969. Stub source states no cause.

name: St. Charles Seminary (Carthagena, Ohio)
notes: Missionaries of the Precious Blood seminary in Carthagena, Ohio, founded 1861; closed as a seminary in 1969 over declining enrollment (theology students moving to Catholic Theological Union, Chicago). Distinct from the operating St. Charles Borromeo Seminary in Philadelphia.

name: Crane Theological School
notes: Divinity school of the still-operating Tufts University in Medford, Massachusetts, founded 1869; closed in 1968 for lack of funds, its endowment redirected to Tufts's religion department and chaplaincy.

name: San Luis Rey College
notes: Franciscan college in Oceanside, California, accredited from 1950; closed in 1968 and its seminary relocated to Berkeley as the Franciscan School of Theology, now part of the Graduate Theological Union. Source states no cause.

name: Gibbs Junior College
notes: The first and most successful of Florida's segregated Black public junior colleges, in St. Petersburg, founded 1957; placed under St. Petersburg Junior College in 1964 and fully merged into it by 1967 as Florida desegregated its junior-college system.

name: Fenn College
notes: Private college in Cleveland, Ohio, founded 1923 out of the Cleveland YMCA schools; in 1964 the State of Ohio bought its campus to create the still-operating Cleveland State University, which opened in 1965.

name: Booker T. Washington Junior College
notes: Florida's first and longest-lasting segregated Black public junior college, in Pensacola, founded 1949; closed in 1965 amid desegregation of the junior-college system.

name: Johnson Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Leesburg, Florida, opened 1962 alongside the white Lake-Sumter Junior College; absorbed into Lake-Sumter (now Lake-Sumter State College) by the 1966-67 year amid desegregation.

name: Volusia County Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Daytona Beach, Florida, founded 1958; closed on short notice in 1965 and merged with the white Daytona Beach Junior College, now the still-operating Daytona State College.

name: Roosevelt Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in West Palm Beach, Florida, founded 1958; abruptly closed by the county board in 1965 amid desegregation, with no merger into Palm Beach Junior College (only six faculty transferred).

name: Collier-Blocker Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Palatka, Florida, founded 1960; the least-enrolled and shortest-lived of Florida's Black junior colleges, merged into St. Johns River Junior College in 1966.

name: Suwannee River Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Madison, Florida, founded 1959; merged into North Florida Junior College in 1966 amid desegregation.

name: Rosenwald Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Panama City, Florida, founded 1958; merged into Gulf Coast Junior College (now Gulf Coast State College) in 1966 amid desegregation.

name: Hampton Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Ocala, Florida, founded 1958; the last of Florida's twelve Black junior colleges to be merged, into Central Florida Junior College (now the College of Central Florida) in 1966.

name: Jackson Junior College
notes: Segregated Black public junior college in Marianna, Florida, opened 1961; closed in 1966 during desegregation, its students (unlike other Florida cases) not transitioned to the white Chipola Junior College.

name: Honolulu Christian College
notes: Christian college in Honolulu, Hawaii, established 1949; merged in September 1966 into Hawaii Pacific College, now the still-operating Hawaii Pacific University. Source (a one-sentence mention) states no cause or level.

name: Bradford Durfee College of Technology
notes: Public technical college in Fall River, Massachusetts, founded 1899 (bachelor's from 1947); merged with the New Bedford Institute of Technology to form the Southeastern Massachusetts Technological Institute, now the still-operating University of Massachusetts Dartmouth.

name: New Bedford Institute of Technology
notes: Public technical college in New Bedford, Massachusetts, founded 1899; its 1964 merger with Bradford Durfee College formed the Southeastern Massachusetts Technological Institute, now the still-operating University of Massachusetts Dartmouth.

name: West Baden College
notes: Jesuit theologate at West Baden Springs, Indiana (associated with Loyola University Chicago), operating 1934-1964; closed after the 1963-64 year over low enrollment and escalating maintenance costs, the property sold in 1966.

name: Chouinard Art Institute
notes: Art school in Los Angeles, California, founded 1921; in 1961 it merged (under Walt and Roy Disney) with the Los Angeles Conservatory of Music to form the still-operating California Institute of the Arts, continuing to operate until the CalArts campus opened in 1970.

name: Conservatory of Music of Kansas City
notes: Degree-granting music conservatory in Kansas City, Missouri (predecessor founded 1906; reorganized 1926); merged September 1, 1959 into the University of Kansas City, now the still-operating University of Missouri-Kansas City.

name: Cincinnati Conservatory of Music
notes: Music conservatory in Cincinnati, Ohio, founded 1867; merged in 1955 with the College of Music of Cincinnati to form the Cincinnati College-Conservatory of Music, now part of the still-operating University of Cincinnati. Source states no cause.

name: College of Music of Cincinnati
notes: Degree-granting music college in Cincinnati, Ohio, founded 1878; its operating costs exceeded income by 1954 and it merged in May 1955 with the Cincinnati Conservatory of Music to form the Cincinnati College-Conservatory of Music.

name: Jepson Art Institute
notes: Art school in Los Angeles, California, founded 1945; closed 1954. Source states no cause or nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: Black Mountain College
notes: Famed experimental liberal-arts college in Black Mountain, North Carolina, founded 1933; suspended classes by court order over debts and closed in 1957 as enrollment collapsed.

name: Bishop Payne Divinity School
notes: Black Episcopal seminary in Petersburg, Virginia, founded 1878; after Virginia Theological Seminary began admitting Black students in 1951, its assets and records transferred there June 3, 1953.

name: Junior College of Bergen County
notes: Junior college in Teaneck, New Jersey (earlier Hackensack), founded 1933; merged in late 1953 into Fairleigh Dickinson College, now the still-operating Fairleigh Dickinson University. Source does not clearly state public/private control.

name: Blackstone College for Girls
notes: Methodist women's institution in Blackstone, Virginia, chartered 1892 (a secondary school that added a women's junior college from 1915-16); dwindling enrollment and the Korean War forced it to close in 1950.

name: Miner Normal School
notes: Black public teacher-training school in Washington, D.C., founded 1851 by Myrtilla Miner (a four-year college from 1929); merged in 1955 with Wilson Teachers College to form the District of Columbia Teachers College (which itself merged into UDC in 1977).

name: Beda-Etta College
notes: School for students of color in Macon, Georgia, founded 1921, combining a two-year junior college with a commercial high school; closed 1955. Source states no cause.

name: National Conservatory of Music of America
notes: Degree-granting music institution in New York City, founded 1885 by Jeannette Thurber (where Dvorak taught); it ceased practical operations by about 1930 and was declared defunct by New York State in 1952 as its philanthropic support faded.

name: Middlesex University (Massachusetts)
notes: Private university in Waltham, Massachusetts, founded 1914 (with medical, veterinary, and liberal-arts schools); after a 1944 state law required an AMA-accredited MD, it closed in 1947 and its campus and charter were used to found Brandeis University in 1948.

name: North Pacific College
notes: Professional dental, pharmacy, and optometry college in Portland, Oregon, founded 1899; after the American Dental Association denied its dental school accreditation in 1944, it merged in 1945 into the University of Oregon (now OHSU School of Dentistry), its optometry program going to Pacific University.

name: Indiana Law School
notes: Law school in Indianapolis, Indiana, founded 1894; after a 1936 merger with the Benjamin Harrison Law School it became part of Indiana University in 1944, now the still-operating IU Robert H. McKinney School of Law.

name: Spokane Junior College
notes: Junior college in Spokane, Washington, founded 1935 (a reorganization of the earlier Spokane University); facing wartime enrollment decline and rising costs, it shut down and merged in February 1942 into the still-operating Whitworth College (now Whitworth University).

name: Massachusetts State College-Fort Devens
notes: Temporary WWII-veterans' branch of Massachusetts State College (now the University of Massachusetts Amherst) at Fort Devens in Ayer, Massachusetts, opened 1946 (1,700 students); enrollment fell sharply and it closed after the 1948-49 year.

name: Eastern State Normal School
notes: Public teacher-training normal school in Castine, Maine, founded 1867; closed in 1942, its buildings taken over by the Maine Maritime Academy. Stub source states no cause.

name: Fairmont Seminary
notes: Girls' boarding school in Washington, D.C., founded 1899, combining a preparatory school with a junior college (renamed Fairmont Junior College and Preparatory School for Girls in 1923); closed December 1942 amid financial trouble, about 100 students moving to Casements Junior College. Primarily a finishing/prep school with a junior-college tier.

name: Texas Military College
notes: Private junior college (with high-school and primary divisions) in Terrell, Texas, operating 1915-1949; its property was later sold to Southern Bible Institute. Source states no cause.

name: Howard-Payne Junior College
notes: Methodist women's junior college in Fayette, Missouri, opened 1859 (chartered as Howard Female College); closed in 1927 during a consolidation of small Methodist colleges, its buildings absorbed by the still-operating Central Methodist University.

name: Claver College
notes: Black Catholic college in Guthrie, Oklahoma, founded 1933 by the Benedictine Sisters of St. Joseph's Monastery (Tulsa) as a night school of higher education; closed 1944. Source states no cause.

name: Rutersville College
notes: Texas's first institution of higher education, a Methodist college in Rutersville, chartered 1840 under the Republic of Texas (194 students in 1844); financial instability led it to be succeeded by Soule University in 1856 (lineage later to Southwestern University).

name: Soule University
notes: Methodist university in Chappell Hill, Texas, founded 1856 (successor to Rutersville College); beset by post-Civil War finances and yellow-fever epidemics, its sponsors formed Southwestern University as a replacement (chartered 1873) and Soule closed in 1887.

name: Salado College
notes: Coeducational college in Salado, Texas, incorporated 1860 (307 students in 1865); the first Texas college to run without church or state funds, sustained only by tuition, it closed in 1885 (the site later a high school).

name: Waco Female College
notes: Methodist women's institution in Waco, Texas, chartered 1854 (202 students in 1893), running preparatory, primary, and collegiate departments; closed 1895 for financial reasons, its buildings bought by the Add-Ran (TCU) predecessor. Mixed-level, not a clean postsecondary college.

name: Belle Plain College
notes: Methodist college in the now-defunct town of Belle Plain, Texas, founded 1881 (over 300 students at its height); when the railroad bypassed the town for Baird its population collapsed, a bank foreclosed in 1889, and it closed by 1892.

name: Fort Worth University
notes: Methodist university in Fort Worth, Texas, founded 1881 (871 students in 1908, with medical and law schools); its liberal-arts department merged in 1911 into the Methodist University of Oklahoma, now the still-operating Oklahoma City University.

name: Fort Worth School of Medicine
notes: Medical school in Fort Worth, Texas, founded 1894 out of the separately chartered Fort Worth University; after the university merged away in 1911 the medical school continued until 1919, when it merged with the still-operating Texas Christian University.

name: St. Mary's University (Galveston, Texas)
notes: Roman Catholic university and seminary in Galveston, Texas, founded 1855, later run by the Jesuits; closed in 1922 when the Jesuits left Galveston to concentrate resources in New Orleans (the seminary relocated, charter transferred 1926). Distinct from the still-operating St. Mary's University in San Antonio.

name: University of San Antonio
notes: Methodist university in San Antonio, Texas, founded 1894 as San Antonio Female College (later Westmoorland College); merged in 1942 into the still-operating Trinity University, which adopted its alumni. Distinct from the modern University of Texas at San Antonio.

name: University of San Augustine (Texas)
notes: One of the earliest Texas colleges, in San Augustine, founded 1837 (150 students); a bitter local rivalry with Wesleyan College forced both to close, with a proposed 1847 merger into a University of Eastern Texas failing by 1851.

name: McKenzie College (Texas)
notes: Methodist college in Clarksville, Texas, founded 1841 (the largest Texas college of the 1850s and 1860s, 300+ students in 1854); unable to sustain itself financially after the Civil War, it closed June 25, 1868. Distinct from McKenzie College in Tennessee.

name: South Texas Junior College
notes: YMCA-affiliated junior college in Houston, Texas, founded 1948 (nearly 5,000 students in the late 1960s); the University of Houston acquired its assets August 6, 1974 to open the still-operating University of Houston-Downtown.

name: Juarez-Lincoln University
notes: Chicano-movement university founded 1971 (Fort Worth, then Austin), Texas, affiliated with Antioch College (over 500 students); it closed in 1979 when Antioch withdrew its funding.

name: Jacinto Trevino College
notes: Chicano-movement college founded 1969 in Mercedes, Texas, by Mexican Americans who felt underserved; 1971 political disputes cost it staff and students (some leaving to found Juarez-Lincoln University) and it closed in the mid-1970s (exact year not stated).

name: Westminster College (Texas)
notes: Methodist Protestant college in Westminster, Texas, founded 1888 (a preparatory school, then a junior college, later offering a four-year religion degree); its college-level part merged into the still-operating Southwestern University in 1942, the Texas residual closing in 1950.

name: Cane Hill College
notes: The first institution of higher learning in Arkansas, a Cumberland Presbyterian college at Canehill, tracing to 1834; competition from the new University of Arkansas and an 1885 fire ended it at Cane Hill in 1891, its lineage continuing as Arkansas Cumberland College, now the still-operating University of the Ozarks.

name: St. Johns' College (Arkansas)
notes: Masonic college in Little Rock, Arkansas, chartered 1850 and opened 1859 (142 students in 1881), with college, preparatory, military, and primary departments; the Grand Lodge withdrew support in 1878, classes ended by 1882, and the campus burned in 1890.

name: Northrop University
notes: Aeronautics and engineering university in Inglewood, California, founded 1945 by the Northrop Aircraft Corporation; ended its degree programs after June 1991 amid low enrollment and financial problems (a non-degree training successor followed).

name: Upland College
notes: Brethren in Christ college in Upland, California, operating since the 1920s; in 1964 Messiah College (now the still-operating Messiah University, Pennsylvania) took over its operations and consolidated them east.

name: Nairobi College
notes: Community junior college for ethnic-minority students in East Palo Alto, California, founded 1969 (Wikipedia credits the Black Panther Party); active until 1981. Source states no cause.

name: Orange County Business College
notes: For-profit business college in Anaheim, California, founded 1973 as an affiliate of Eldorado College; it closed November 24, 1997 when its parent Eldorado College was forced to close.

name: Whittier Law School
notes: Law school of the still-operating Whittier College in Costa Mesa, California, founded 1966; after years of poor bar-passage and job-placement metrics it stopped admitting students in 2017 and ceased operations in 2020.

name: Columbia Pacific University
notes: Unaccredited distance university in Novato, California, founded 1978; it operated for about two decades before a California court ordered it permanently closed on December 2, 1999, state officials calling it a diploma mill. Recorded with that caveat.

name: California Pacific University
notes: ACICS-accredited private university in Escondido (later Pinole), California, founded 1976; closed September 18, 2016 after the state denied renewal of its approval to operate over an annual-report compliance failure.

name: California Southern Law School
notes: State-registered (unaccredited) evening law school in Riverside, California, founded 1971 as Citrus Belt Law School (renamed 1990); took its last entering class in 2016 and closed after the spring 2020 semester.
motto: A Great Value in Legal Education

name: University of Northern California, Lorenzo Patino School of Law
notes: Unaccredited (state-registered) part-time law school in Sacramento, California, founded 1983; the State Bar terminated its registration effective June 30, 2013 amid very low bar-passage rates.
motto: Excellence and Affordability in Legal Education

name: Berean Bible College
notes: Non-accredited Christian college in the San Diego area (Poway), California, founded September 1971; closed permanently in 2018. Recorded with an unaccredited caveat.

name: Graefenberg Medical Institute
notes: The first medical school chartered by the Alabama legislature, at Dadeville, chartered 1852; its last session was 1860 and it closed in 1861 at the onset of the Civil War (records burned 1873).

name: Abingdon College
notes: Disciples of Christ college in Abingdon, Illinois, founded 1853; consolidated in the 1880s (merger 1885, campus closed 1888) with the still-operating Eureka College.

name: Old University of Chicago
notes: The original Baptist University of Chicago, founded 1856 (with law and medical departments); after years of financial struggle and a fire, creditors foreclosed and classes ceased in 1886. Distinct from the modern University of Chicago (1890).

name: Jubilee College
notes: Episcopal college near Peoria (Brimfield), Illinois, founded 1839 by Bishop Philander Chase; it declined after Chase's 1852 death and closed in 1862 (the site is now a state historic site).

name: University of Nauvoo
notes: Latter-day Saint university in Nauvoo, Illinois, founded 1841; the Illinois legislature repealed the Nauvoo Charter in January 1845 and it ended as the Mormons left in 1846. Distinct from a modern namesake.

name: William & Vashti College
notes: Non-denominational college in Aledo, Illinois, founded 1908; closed in 1918 after WWI conscription drained its enrollment (the campus later became a military academy).

name: Westfield College (Illinois)
notes: United Brethren in Christ college in Westfield, Illinois, founded 1861 as a seminary (incorporated as a college 1865; 160 students in 1909); closed 1914 amid enrollment decline.

name: Illinois State University (Springfield, Illinois)
notes: Historical Evangelical Lutheran university, founded 1847 (relocated to Springfield 1852 and renamed Illinois State University); it ceased operations in 1868 and reopened as the still-operating Carthage College in 1870. Distinct from the modern Illinois State University in Normal.

name: Harvey Medical College
notes: Co-educational medical college in Chicago, Illinois, which opened between 1890 and 1910 and (unlike many contemporaries) offered a real education; now defunct. Source states no founding year, closure year, or cause.

name: Northwestern University Woman's Medical School
notes: Women's medical school in Chicago, founded 1870 as the Woman's Hospital Medical College; it became part of the still-operating Northwestern University in 1891 and the university closed it in 1902.

name: Bush Conservatory of Music
notes: Degree-granting music conservatory in Chicago, founded 1901 (Bachelor of Music); under Depression financial duress it merged in 1932 into the Chicago Conservatory College (which itself later closed in 1981).

name: The Chicago Conservatory College
notes: Chicago music school and conservatory tracing to 1857 (it absorbed the Bush Conservatory in 1932); operated until 1981. Source states no cause (reportedly in good standing at closure).

name: Ellis University
notes: For-profit online university in Oakbrook Terrace, Illinois (Ellis University name from 2008; 1,338 students); ceased operations December 1, 2016 after DEAC withdrew its accreditation.

name: Eleutherian College
notes: Anti-slavery college in Lancaster, Indiana, founded 1848 (college-level work from 1854; the first Indiana college to admit Black students and women); closed 1874. Began as a secondary institute. Source states no cause.

name: Hartsville College
notes: United Brethren college in Hartsville, Indiana, chartered 1850; absorbed July 15, 1897 into the newly created Central College, now the still-operating Huntington University.

name: Liber College
notes: Share-funded college in Liber, Indiana, founded 1853 (156 students in 1860-61), teaching both collegiate and primary students; closed in the 1870s (sources vary 1873/1880). Source states no cause or control.

name: Anthony Wayne Institute
notes: Two-year commercial (business) college in Fort Wayne, Indiana, founded about 1916; closed in 1933 during the Great Depression.

name: Valparaiso Technical Institute
notes: Technical institute in Valparaiso, Indiana, tracing to 1874 (electronics, radio, and telegraph engineering; once the largest telegraph school in the US); closed April 1991 after a staffing collapse. Source states no clear cause or nonprofit/for-profit control.

name: Oskaloosa College
notes: Disciples of Christ liberal-arts college in Oskaloosa, Iowa, tracing to 1855 (classes from 1861); it lost most of its faculty and students to the new Drake University in 1881 and closed in 1898 amid financial hardship.

name: Western College (Iowa)
notes: United Brethren college founded 1857 (the denomination's first west of the Mississippi; relocated to Toledo, Iowa in 1881; renamed Leander Clark College in 1906); bankruptcy led it to merge in 1919 into the still-operating Coe College.

name: Cleveland University
notes: The first higher-education institution in Cleveland, Ohio, founded 1851 by former Oberlin president Asa Mahan (coeducational and open to all races); closed by the end of 1853 amid internal conflict, having graduated only 11 students. Source states no cause.

name: Franklin College (New Athens, Ohio)
notes: College in New Athens, Ohio, founded 1818; it ceased operation in 1919 and its records were absorbed by Muskingum College. Source states no cause.

name: National Normal University
notes: Teacher-training university in Lebanon, Ohio, founded 1855 as the Southwestern Normal School (named National Normal University in 1870); it went bankrupt and merged in 1917 into the still-operating Wilmington College.

name: Ohio Central College
notes: College in Iberia, Ohio, founded 1854 by the Free Presbyterian Church, open to all regardless of race or gender; it ended classes in the late 19th century (records absorbed by Muskingum College). Source states no closure year or cause.

name: Ohio Wesleyan Female College
notes: One of the oldest women's colleges in the US, in Delaware, Ohio, founded 1850 as an academy (college status 1853); merged in 1877 into the still-operating Ohio Wesleyan University.

name: Ohio State and Union Law College
notes: Proprietary law school founded 1855 as the Poland Law College in Poland, Ohio (later Cleveland), owner-operated by John Crowell (about 500 students over its life); closed in 1876 when Crowell retired.

name: Atlanta Conservatory of Music
notes: Degree-granting music conservatory in Atlanta, Georgia, founded 1907 (900 students in 1922); a fire destroyed its building on November 18, 1936, killing three students, and it closed about three years later.

name: Lanier University
notes: Baptist university in Atlanta, Georgia, founded 1917; plagued by financial problems, it was sold to the Ku Klux Klan in 1921 and closed September 1, 1922.

name: University of Atlanta
notes: For-profit online university (founded in the early 1990s as Barrington University, relocated to Atlanta, Georgia in 2008); it resigned its accreditation June 30, 2013 after stopping new enrollment and an investigation found its chairman's advertised degrees were fabricated.

name: Hawaii College of Pharmacy
notes: Unaccredited for-profit Pharm.D. school in Hawaii; the state shut it down for fraud (falsely assuring some 240 students that accreditation was forthcoming while taking tuition) and barred its owners from Hawaii business. Source states no founding or closure year.

name: Princeton Law School
notes: Short-lived law department of the College of New Jersey (now the still-operating Princeton University), founded 1847; only seven students earned a law degree before it closed in 1852.

name: Lincoln Business College
notes: For-profit business college in Lincoln, Nebraska, founded 1884; merged in 1925 into the Lincoln School of Commerce, which through later acquisitions became Hamilton College, Kaplan University, and finally Purdue University Global (Lincoln), closing in 2021.

name: Redstone College
parent_name: Spartan College of Aeronautics and Technology
notes: For-profit college in Broomfield, Colorado (owned by Alta Colleges); after its ACICS accreditation was revoked, its campus was acquired in 2016 by the Spartan Education Group and now operates as a Spartan College of Aeronautics and Technology campus.

name: Folsom Business College
notes: Business college founded 1848 by Ezekiel G. Folsom in Cleveland, Ohio; it was purchased by the founders of Bryant & Stratton and absorbed into the still-operating Bryant & Stratton chain. No standalone article; year not stated.

name: St. John's College, Cleveland
notes: Roman Catholic college for teachers and nurses in Cleveland, Ohio, established 1928 as Sisters' College (670 students in fall 1974); closed 1975, its nursing program moving to Ursuline College. Source states no cause.

name: St. John's College (Toledo, Ohio)
notes: Jesuit college (with a law school) in downtown Toledo, Ohio, founded 1898; the college closed during the Great Depression, and the site reopened in 1965 as the secondary St. John's Jesuit High School. Source gives no exact college-closure year.

name: Wadsworth Institute
notes: General Conference Mennonite seminary in Wadsworth, Ohio, founded 1868 (the first major cooperative Mennonite school in North America; ~34 students a year); closed 1878 amid low attendance and debt.

name: Aakers Business College
notes: For-profit two-year business college in Fargo, North Dakota (later Grand Forks and Bismarck), founded 1902; merged in 2007 into the still-operating Rasmussen College.

name: Yadkin College
notes: Methodist Protestant college in the Yadkin College community of Davidson County, North Carolina, founded 1857 (a college 1857-1883); it declined to academy and high-school level and closed in 1924 as public high schools rose.

name: Elizabeth College (Virginia)
notes: Women's liberal-arts college founded 1896 in Charlotte, North Carolina (moved to Salem, Virginia in 1915); after its campus burned under suspicious circumstances in December 1921 it closed in 1922, Roanoke College adopting its alumnae.

name: Blue Mont Central College
notes: Methodist college incorporated 1858 in Manhattan, Kansas; in 1863 its building and 120 acres were transferred to the state to found the land-grant college, now the still-operating Kansas State University.

name: Highland University
notes: Presbyterian college in Highland, Kansas (origins stated as ~1837), which rejected George Washington Carver on arrival because of his race; now defunct (Highland Community College claims descent from it). Source gives no closure year or cause.

name: Garfield University
notes: Disciples of Christ university in Wichita, Kansas, founded 1887 (named for President Garfield); financial difficulty closed it in 1890, a 1892 reopening failed, and it closed for good November 18, 1893 (its building later became Friends University).

name: Harper College (Kansas)
notes: Churches of Christ college in Harper, Kansas; in April 1924 it merged with Arkansas Christian College to form Harding College, now the still-operating Harding University in Searcy, Arkansas.

name: Algona College
notes: Methodist college in Algona, Iowa, founded 1869; its endowment fundraising collapsed amid the 1870s grasshopper-plague crop devastation and it closed in 1875.

name: Grundy College
notes: Christian Reformed Church school in Grundy Center, Iowa, founded 1916, combining a high-school academy with a junior college and commercial department; closed 1934 amid Depression finances and inter-institutional rivalries.

name: Marycrest College
notes: Catholic women's (later coeducational) college in Davenport, Iowa, founded 1939 (935 students in 1961; later Teikyo Marycrest, then Marycrest International University); closed in 2002 amid enrollment decline and financial difficulty.

name: Coral Ridge Baptist University
notes: Unaccredited Baptist Bible college and seminary in Jacksonville, Florida, founded 1985; merged in 2001 into Freedom University and Seminary. Recorded with an unaccredited caveat.
motto: I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.

name: Jones College (Florida)
notes: Nonprofit business/junior college in Jacksonville, Florida, founded 1918; it closed December 31, 2017 after its accreditor ACICS lost federal recognition.

name: Ruskin Colleges
notes: Cooperative/socialist college at Ruskin, Florida (opened 1910; part of a Ruskin college movement also in Missouri and Illinois); most of the college burned in 1919 and it closed when founder George Miller died later that year.

name: South Florida Military College
notes: Degree-granting college in Bartow, Florida, founded 1895 (degree authority from 1903); abolished by the 1905 Buckman Act that consolidated Florida's higher education, with equipment transferred to the still-operating University of Florida.

name: Southwest Florida College
notes: For-profit career college in Fort Myers, Florida, founded 1974; acquired in 2014 by Southern Technical College Suncoast and rebranded as the still-operating Southern Technical College.

name: Arcadia College
notes: Methodist college in Arcadia, Missouri, founded 1843; closed 1877 (the site later ran an Ursuline academy to 1971). Source states no cause.

name: Central Female College
notes: Methodist women's college in Lexington, Missouri, founded 1869 (as Marvin Female Institute); its sponsoring conferences closed it after spring 1925, the property going to Central College.

name: Clarksburg College
notes: College in Clarksburg, Missouri, founded 1877 (as Clarksburg Academy), granting degrees by the 1890s; later closed (year not stated), graduates transferring to Central College.

name: Douglass University
notes: Historically Black university in St. Louis, Missouri, founded 1926 (law, theology, business, music; the second Missouri university to admit Black students); it struggled through the Depression, closed by 1942, briefly reopened in 1943, and did not survive.

name: Fulton Female Synodical College
notes: Presbyterian women's college in Fulton, Missouri, operating 1873-1928; closed when the church redirected its support to another institution.

name: Kemper College
notes: Episcopal liberal-arts college near St. Louis, Missouri, chartered 1837; closed in 1845 under over-expansion and debt, only its medical department surviving (it later became the Washington University School of Medicine).

name: Marion College (Missouri)
notes: Presbyterian manual-labor college in Marion County, Missouri, founded 1831; the Panic of 1837 and a burst land-speculation bubble collapsed its enrollment and it closed in spring 1844 (the campus bought by the Masonic College of Missouri).

name: Pritchett College
notes: Non-denominational Christian college in Glasgow, Missouri, founded 1866 (~200 students in 1869); it dropped upper-level courses after 1917 to become a junior college and closed in June 1922.

name: Asbury College (Maryland)
notes: Methodist college in Baltimore, Maryland, founded 1816; it closed in the 1830s (still operating in 1832). Stub source states no exact year or cause.

name: Baltimore College
notes: Secular college in Baltimore, Maryland, founded 1804; in the early 1820s it merged into what became the University of Maryland, Baltimore. Source gives no exact merger year.

name: Calvert College
notes: Catholic-operated college in New Windsor, Maryland, operating 1852-1873 (the site later became a preparatory school). Stub source states no level or cause.

name: Chevy Chase Junior College
notes: Women's junior college in Chevy Chase, Maryland, operating 1903-1950 (119 students in 1946); it did not reopen after August 1950 amid low enrollment, rising costs, and Korean War uncertainty.

name: Cokesbury College
notes: The first Methodist college in the United States, in Abingdon (later Baltimore), Maryland, founded 1787; it closed December 4, 1796 when its Baltimore building burned down.

name: Mount Hope College (Maryland)
notes: College on the outskirts of Baltimore, Maryland, founded 1833; closed 1844. Stub source states no cause.

name: New Windsor College
notes: New Windsor, Maryland, hosted two successive colleges of this name: the first (1843-1851) closed, and the second (1876-1912) was absorbed into Blue Ridge College (which itself later closed in 1944).

name: Washington Medical College
notes: Medical school in Baltimore, Maryland, founded 1827 (later Washington University of Baltimore); after a first closure in 1851 and 1867 revival, it merged in 1878 into the College of Physicians and Surgeons (later part of the University of Maryland).

name: Central Mississippi College
notes: Baptist school in Kosciusko, Mississippi, founded 1893; ran as a grammar/high/normal school and later a junior college (336 students in 1908). Closure year not stated by the source; recorded on its junior-college basis.

name: Madison College (Mississippi)
notes: Degree-granting college in Sharon, Mississippi, founded 1851 (it absorbed the charter of Brandon College); ceased operations in 1872 for want of endowment and patronage.

name: Oakland College (Mississippi)
notes: Presbyterian men's college near Rodney, Mississippi, founded 1830; disrupted by the Civil War (students and faculty joining the Confederacy), it closed in 1871 and its campus was bought by the state to found Alcorn State University.

name: Sharon Female College
notes: Methodist women's college in Sharon, Mississippi, founded 1837 (reincorporated 1846); it survived the Civil War but declined under post-war regional economic stress and closed in 1873.

name: St. Charles College (Missouri)
notes: Methodist college in St. Charles, Missouri, founded 1837 (a military school from 1901); closed 1915, its grounds later a public high school. Distinct from the same-named colleges in Maryland and Louisiana. Source states no cause.

name: St. Joseph Female College
notes: Baptist women's college in St. Joseph, Missouri, opened 1875; closed 1881. Source states no cause.

name: Woman's Medical College of St. Louis
notes: The first college west of the Mississippi to educate women in medicine, in St. Louis, Missouri, first founded 1883 and re-established 1891; closed 1896 amid the Panic of 1893.

name: Dodd College
notes: Baptist junior college for women in Shreveport, Louisiana, founded 1927 by the radio preacher Monroe E. Dodd; closed 1942. Source states no cause.

name: Lake Charles College
notes: Congregationalist college in Lake Charles, Louisiana, incorporated 1887 (most students in its preparatory department); closed by 1902 amid insufficient enrollment and finances, the site becoming Lake Charles High School.

name: Cobb Divinity School
notes: Free Will Baptist divinity school founded 1840 in Parsonsfield, Maine (later Lewiston); affiliated with Bates College from 1870, it disbanded in 1908 and became the still-operating Bates College's religion department.

name: Medical School of Maine
notes: The medical department of the still-operating Bowdoin College in Brunswick, Maine, founded 1821; Bowdoin closed it in 1921.

name: Bristol College (Pennsylvania)
notes: Episcopal college near Bristol (Croydon), Bucks County, Pennsylvania, established 1833; closed February 1837 for lack of financial support.

name: Log College
notes: The first Presbyterian ministerial school in North America, at Warminster, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, founded 1727 by William Tennent; it closed on his death about 1746 and was a forerunner of Princeton. A ministerial log-cabin school, not a chartered degree college.

name: Maimonides College
notes: The first Jewish institution of higher learning in the United States, a theological seminary in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, founded 1867; closed December 1873 amid financial difficulty.

name: Polytechnic College of Pennsylvania
notes: Engineering college in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, founded 1853 (the eighth US engineering school, the first to offer mechanical-engineering, mining, and architecture degrees); closed 1890.

name: Spring Garden College
notes: College in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, founded 1851 as the Spring Garden Institute; declining enrollment and financial problems forced its closure in 1992.

name: Central University of Kentucky
notes: Presbyterian university in Richmond, Kentucky, chartered 1873; beset by finances and small enrollment, it consolidated July 16, 1901 into the still-operating Centre College.

name: Augusta College (Kentucky)
notes: The third Methodist college founded in the United States, in Augusta, Kentucky, founded 1822 (~305 students); closed 1849. Source states no cause.

name: Louisville College of Pharmacy
notes: Pharmacy college in Louisville, Kentucky, founded 1870; merged in 1947 into the University of Kentucky (relocated to Lexington in 1957 as the still-operating UK College of Pharmacy).

name: Bolivar College
notes: Institution in Madisonville, Tennessee, founded 1825, running as both a preparatory school and a college (100 students in 1904); closed December 1907, the property becoming the county's first public high school. Mixed prep-and-college level.

name: Franklin College (Tennessee)
notes: Disciples of Christ college in Davidson County (Nashville), Tennessee, founded 1844 by Tolbert Fanning; disrupted when most students joined the Confederate army, it closed around 1861 (its building later burned).

name: Neophogen College
notes: College in Cross Plains, then Gallatin, Tennessee, founded 1873 (250 students after moving to Gallatin), noted for etiquette and English instruction; closed at the end of 1878. Source states no cause.

name: Scarritt College for Christian Workers
notes: Methodist college for Christian workers, founded 1892 in Kansas City and moved to Nashville, Tennessee in 1924 (a graduate school from 1981); closed in 1988, the campus becoming the non-degree Scarritt Bennett Center.

name: University of Nashville
notes: Historic Nashville, Tennessee, university tracing to 1806 (Cumberland College); it ran medical, military, literary, and preparatory schools and dispersed as a distinct entity by 1909 -- its medical school into Vanderbilt (1874), its Peabody Normal line into George Peabody College (later merged into the still-operating Vanderbilt University), and Montgomery Bell Academy surviving as a prep school.

name: Walden University (Tennessee)
notes: Historically Black Methodist university in Nashville, Tennessee, founded 1865 for freedmen (a junior college from 1922); closed 1925 amid financial difficulty and competition with state colleges. Distinct from the modern online Walden University.

name: Jackson College (Tennessee)
notes: Presbyterian college founded 1830 (as a manual-labor academy) at Spring Hill, Tennessee, moved to Columbia in 1837; burned by the Union Army during the Civil War and closed around 1863. Distinct from the historically Black Jackson College in Mississippi.
